1	Introduction
     2	 The Apgar score is based on five components (skin color, heart rate, reflex irritability, muscle
     3	tone, and respiration). Each item is scored from 0 to 2 with a total score of 7–10 as normal and the
     4	highest score of 10 representing the optimal condition. The Apgar score has been used worldwide as a
     5	vitality index for almost every newborn immediately after birth.
     6	
     7	
     8	
     9	
    10	 Methods
    11	 Study Population
    12	 We conducted a population-based cohort study using data from Danish national registers. A total of
    13	2,272,473 live singletons were identified during 1978–2015 from the Danish Medical Birth Registry .
    14	We excluded 1,001 births with missing information on sex and 41,252 births with no valid information
    15	on 5-min Apgar scores (including the score of 0). We further excluded 16,398 infants who died or
    16	emigrated from Denmark before the age of 1 year. The final cohort comprised 2,213,822 births.
    17	
    18	
    19	
    20	
    21	 Discussion
    22	 Main Findings
    23	 In this large population-based cohort study, during childhood, we found individuals with even
    24	clinically “normal” Apgar score range of 7–9 still had higher risks of overall mental disorders and
    25	some specific diagnoses: organic disorders and a series of neurodevelopmental disorders
    26	(intellectual disability, pervasive developmental disorders, childhood autism, and ADHD). It is also
    27	interesting to observe that compromised Apgar scores were at elevated risks of developing organic
    28	disorders and neurotic disorders, which were reported for the first time. During early adulthood,
    29	compromised 5-min Apgar scores were not found to be associated with mental disorders.
    30	
    31	
    32	 Comparisons With Other Studies
    33	 To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the association of the full spectrum of mental
    34	disorders with the 5-min Apgar score. Our findings indicate the strongest associations for
    35	intellectual disability in childhood, which corroborates the results from previous studies. Most
    36	previous studies were based on results of different non-standardized intelligence tests, and
    37	cross-sectional or descriptive designs, except a recent Swedish study, by virtue of clinically
    38	confirmed diagnosis and cohort design, reporting that term infants with low 5-min Apgar score had a
    39	higher risk of severe neurologic morbidity, including a 9-fold risk of intellectual disability.
    40	However, the Swedish study only captured cases before 14 years of age and only adjusted for year of
    41	birth, maternal age, parity, and smoking. Similarly, we observed 3~5-fold risks of intellectual
    42	disability in childhood (until 18 years of age), and we were able to adjust for not only the
    43	aforementioned confounders but also parental psychiatric history and socioeconomic status,
    44	indicating a more robust association. In addition, ADHD and autism were another two widely studied
    45	neurodevelopment disorders in relation to Apgar score during childhood, but existing results were
    46	inconsistent, which may be due to heterogeneity of methodology, in particular categorizations of
    47	Apgar scores and definition of outcomes. For example, some studies used pervasive developmental
    48	disorder (ICD-10 codes: F84) as a proxy to define autism, which includes but is not limited to
    49	autism. To reduce the possibility of misclassification, we only focused on childhood autism–the
    50	typical and most severe type of autism–to explore the association. Our findings further support that
    51	compromised 5-min Apgar scores were associated with childhood autism.
    52	
    53	
    54	 Furthermore, we observed that individuals with a compromised 5-min Apgar score had higher risks of
    55	organic disorder and neurotic disorder during childhood, which have not been reported previously.
    56	These findings imply that less-than-optimal Apgar scores at birth may be an indicator for a broad
    57	scope of mental disorders in childhood, not merely neurodevelopmental disorders.
    58	
    59	
    60	 There have been scarce studies examining the association between low Apgar score and adulthood
    61	mental health. We did not find that compromised 5-min Apgar scores were associated with mental
    62	disorders during early adulthood, which may be attributed to incomplete records of Apgar scores
    63	during the initial establishment of the Danish Medical Birth Register (MBR). We observed that
    64	participants with suboptimal Apgar scores at 5 min tended to have higher risks of organic disorders,
    65	schizophrenia, neurotic disorders, and personality disorders, and the low statistical precisions may
    66	probably be due to limited cases in the low Apgar score groups. Considering that the maximum
    67	attained age in our study was only up to 39 years, the follow-up between 19 and 39 years was not
    68	long enough to detect some late-onset mental disorders (e.g., dementia), therefore, future studies
    69	with extended follow-up to late adulthood are warranted.
    70	
    71	
    72	 Current guidelines recommend Apgar scores of 7 or higher to be reassuring, hence, infants with
    73	these scores are often assumed to constitute a homogeneous group. Nevertheless, recent studies
    74	showed that even reassuring Apgar scores of 7–9 are associated with higher risks of neonatal
    75	mortality, neonatal morbidity, and adverse long-term neurological outcomes, compared with an Apgar
    76	score of 10. We found a dose-response increasing the overall risk of mental disorders with
    77	decreasing Apgar score of 9 toward 7. Furthermore, individuals with “normal” scores of 7–9 carried
    78	increased risks of a wide range of neurodevelopmental disorders, such as intellectual disability,
    79	pervasive developmental disorders, childhood autism, and ADHD. Similarly, prior studies based on
    80	developmental screening scales found children aged 5 years with 5-min Apgar scores of 7–9 were more
    81	vulnerable on the emotional or physical health domain of the Early Development Instrument. Recently,
    82	a large transnational study also suggested that low Apgar scores of 7–9 were associated with a
    83	higher risk of autistic disorder but without controlling for socioeconomic status and paternal
    84	psychiatric history. Our findings are in line with those of previous studies by showing that
    85	reassuring Apgar scores 7–9 are associated with various neurodevelopmental disorders in childhood.
    86	These findings support that 5-min Apgar scores routinely available in contemporary neonatal
    87	settings, even within the normal range 7–9, are not totally reassuring.
    88	
    89	
    90	 The causes of mental disorders are multifactorial. Adverse prenatal events (e.g., gestational
    91	diabetes mellitus, preterm, and restricted fetal growth) are important risk factors and could have a
    92	programming effect on fetal brain development, resulting in increased risk for psychopathology later
    93	in life. In this study, adjusting for gestational age at birth and fetal growth status did not
    94	substantially change the risks, indicating that preterm birth or restricted fetal growth do not
    95	strongly modify the relations between low Apgar scores at birth and subsequent mental disorders.
    96	Although Apgar scores are not clear on any causal pathway of pathogenesis, less-than-optimal Apgar
    97	scores at birth may be a potential sign of the cumulative effect of those adverse prenatal events.
    98	Especially, the clinically reassuring but suboptimal score range 7–9 may indicate subtle but still
    99	detrimental intrauterine insults which will act negatively on fetal brain development. In clinical

100	settings, a distressed infant will receive resuscitation well before the 5-min Apgar score is
   101	assigned, so the score 7–9 could not well reflect severe conditions prior to the assessment. That
   102	may be one of the reasons we observed exposure to the scores 7–9 was associated with an increased
   103	risk of mental disorders. In this study, a novel finding that a compromised 5-min Apgar score was
   104	linked to increased risks of organic disorder and neurotic disorder was reported. Organic disorder
   105	comprises a range of mental disorders based on a demonstrable etiology in cerebral disease, brain
   106	injury, or other insults leading to cerebral dysfunction. Increased risk of organic disorder with
   107	low Apgar score implies adverse prenatal insults (e.g., hypoxia-ischemia, white matter injury,
   108	reduced blood flow, malnutrition) exert a long-lasting impact on brain function in later life. With
   109	regard to neurotic disorder, its prevalence is relevant to low levels of socioeconomic status (SES).
   110	In this study, we found individuals with compromised Apgar scores tended to be born in families with
   111	worse SES (e.g., mothers live alone and have a low education level). It is, therefore, possible that
   112	SES factors at least partially mediate the observed association between compromised Apgar scores and
   113	neurotic disorder.

Based solely on `doc.txt`, here is an explanation of the Apgar score and what the study found about its significance for health outcomes:

## What the Apgar score is

The Apgar score is a "vitality index" used worldwide for almost every newborn immediately after birth. It is based on five components:

1. Skin color
2. Heart rate
3. Reflex irritability
4. Muscle tone
5. Respiration

Each item is scored from 0 to 2, giving a total score. A total of 7–10 is considered normal, with 10 representing the optimal condition.

## The study behind the article

The article describes a large population-based cohort study using Danish national registers. It identified 2,272,473 live singleton births from 1978–2015 in the Danish Medical Birth Registry; after exclusions (missing sex data, missing/invalid 5-minute Apgar scores, and deaths or emigration before age 1), the final cohort comprised 2,213,822 births. To the authors' knowledge, it was the first study to examine the association of the full spectrum of mental disorders with the 5-minute Apgar score.

## Key findings on health outcomes

**Even "normal" scores of 7–9 carry elevated risk.** Current guidelines treat Apgar scores of 7 or higher as reassuring, but the study found that individuals with scores in the clinically "normal" range of 7–9 still had higher risks of:
- Overall mental disorders in childhood
- Organic disorders
- Neurodevelopmental disorders, including intellectual disability, pervasive developmental disorders, childhood autism, and ADHD

There was a dose-response relationship: the overall risk of mental disorders increased as the Apgar score decreased from 9 toward 7. Prior studies also found that scores of 7–9 were associated with higher risks of neonatal mortality, neonatal morbidity, and adverse long-term neurological outcomes compared with a score of 10.

**Compromised (low) scores carry greater risk.** Compromised 5-minute Apgar scores were associated with:
- Intellectual disability in childhood (up to age 18), with 3–5-fold risks — corroborating a Swedish study that reported a 9-fold risk of intellectual disability in term infants with low 5-minute Apgar scores
- Childhood autism (the typical and most severe type)
- Organic disorders and neurotic disorders in childhood — a novel finding reported for the first time in this study

**No association found in early adulthood.** Compromised 5-minute Apgar scores were not found to be associated with mental disorders during early adulthood. The authors suggest this may be due to incomplete Apgar records during the early years of the Danish register, and note that follow-up (up to a maximum attained age of 39) was not long enough to detect late-onset disorders such as dementia.

## Why the association may exist

The authors note that the causes of mental disorders are multifactorial. Adverse prenatal events (e.g., gestational diabetes, preterm birth, restricted fetal growth) can have a "programming effect" on fetal brain development. While the Apgar score does not clarify any causal pathway, a less-than-optimal score at birth may be a potential sign of the cumulative effect of such adverse prenatal events. In particular, the clinically reassuring but suboptimal range of 7–9 may indicate subtle but still detrimental intrauterine insults that negatively affect fetal brain development. Regarding organic disorders specifically, the increased risk with low Apgar scores implies that adverse prenatal insults (e.g., hypoxia-ischemia, white matter injury, reduced blood flow, malnutrition) exert a long-lasting impact on brain function in later life. For neurotic disorders, the authors note that individuals with compromised Apgar scores tended to be born into families with worse socioeconomic status (e.g., mothers living alone with low education), so socioeconomic factors may at least partially mediate that association.

## Practical takeaway

The article's central message is that 5-minute Apgar scores routinely available in contemporary neonatal settings — even within the "normal" range of 7–9 — are not totally reassuring. A less-than-optimal Apgar score at birth may be an indicator for a broad scope of mental disorders in childhood, not merely neurodevelopmental disorders.
